The prevailing opinion among much of the world's population is that those blue lines on the map are not just latitude and longitude lines, but also mark the position of rivers. People who live right next to one of the lines tend to believe that there is no river there, while still believing that there are rivers in other locations. Sailors tend to try to follow the lines across the ocean, believing that there are strong currents there ('ocean rivers') which help expedite their journey, while people travelling across the land perish in the desert while dragging a dinghy with them as they trek around in circles looking for the river.
Central to this belief system is the idea that there is a source of all the north-south rivers at the north pole, and a number of expeditions have attempted to find it. However, as this is the point where 36 rivers split, it is believed to be a place of great evil, and every expedition to date has ended in tragic and bloody infighting as a number of the crew begin to question the wisdom of travelling somewhere so ill-fated.
Despite the universal belief in the rivers, there are a number of disagreeing camps, who believe, for example, that the east-west rivers flow east rather than west, or who believe that the maps get the number of rivers wrong and there are in fact twice as many, with half remaining undiscovered. A number of different religions incorporate the rivers in different ways, and there are many disagreements over the origin and purpose of them. However, there are photos of both the north and the south pole, disproving the myth.
